summary: Gives a fuller specification of the file URI scheme, replacing the short definition in RFC 1738, with a common syntax across existing usage and notes on current practices.

plainLanguage.summary: A file URI is the address form for a file on a computer. This writes down clearly how.

questions: how to write a file url
subtitle: The precise syntax for file: URIs, replacing the one-paragraph definition in RFC 1738.

tldr.problem: The file URI scheme had only a very brief definition in RFC 1738, while real software used it in many slightly different ways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8089 defines the syntax in ABNF on top of the generic URI syntax: an optional host (or the special name localhost) followed by an absolute path. Appendices record the common non-standard variations.
tldr.outcome: It is the Proposed Standard definition of the file scheme and updates RFC 1738. A later RFC, RFC 9844, updates it.

today: RFC 8089 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1738, and it is itself updated by RFC 9844. It is the definition of the file URI scheme registered with IANA.

sections.title: What a File URI Names
sections.content:
A file URI identifies an object (a "file") stored in a structured naming and accessing environment on a host (a "file system"). It can be used when talking about the file and, if other conditions are met, dereferenced to access the file directly.

RFC 8089 replaces the very brief definition in Section 3.10 of RFC 1738. It builds on the generic syntax of RFC 3986 and aims to be compatible with most existing usage. Where it is not, the cause is usually a part that earlier definitions left underspecified.

The scheme is not tied to any particular protocol or media type. Extensions seen in practice are listed in the appendices for information only; implementing them is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: A file URI is a way to point at a file, like writing a room number on a map. This document replaces an older note that was only a few lines long.

sections.title: The File URI Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax is written in ABNF and imports host and path-absolute from RFC 3986. A file URI is the scheme file, a colon, and then either // followed by an optional authority and an absolute path, or just an absolute path (local-path).

The authority, file-auth, is either the string localhost or a host. The host is the fully qualified domain name of the system where the file is accessible. That tells a client on another system that it cannot reach the file system directly, or that it needs some other local mechanism.

localhost means "the machine from which the URI is being interpreted", exactly as if no authority were present. The RFC notes that some software wrongly treats every authority, including localhost, as non-local, and some treats every value as local. For maximum compatibility, creators of URIs MAY write an auth-path with no file-auth.

Case is preserved. Any transport-related handling MUST retain the case as given, and mapping to or from a case-insensitive form is solely the job of the implementation handling the file system.
sections.plainLanguage: A file address says which computer and which path to the file. If you leave the computer part out, it means "this computer". Capital letters stay capital letters.

sections.title: Example Forms
sections.content:
Appendix B shows the forms the syntax is meant to support. For local files, the traditional form has an empty authority, and the minimal form drops the authority and the double slash altogether. For non-local files, the host goes in the authority.

Appendix A points out one difference from RFC 1738: that RFC always began a file URL with file://, followed by an optionally blank host name and a slash. Under RFC 8089 the whole authority component, including the double slashes, is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write the same local file address a short way or a long way. A file on another computer needs that computer's name in it.

sections.title: Operations and Name Encoding
sections.content:
A file URI can be dependably dereferenced, or translated to a local file path, only if it is local: it has no file-auth, or the authority is localhost, or it is a fully qualified domain name that resolves to the machine interpreting the URI. The specification neither defines nor forbids operations on files identified by a non-local file URI.

File systems store names in various encodings, and many modern ones store names as arbitrary octets. When a file URI represents Unicode text, the data SHOULD be encoded as UTF-8 before percent-encoding is applied. Choosing not to use percent-encoded UTF-8 is outside the scope of the RFC and typically needs heuristics or explicit knowledge of how the string will be processed.
sections.plainLanguage: You can only really open a file from an address if the file is on your own computer. Special letters in file names are written in a standard code so every computer reads them the same.

sections.title: Non-Standard Variations in Practice
sections.content:
Appendix E is not normative. It lists variations that existing software meets but that the main syntax does not support, each with a way to extend the grammar if you need to read them.

  • User information: file-auth can be extended with userinfo "@". The RFC warns about this: passwords in userinfo are deprecated by RFC 3986.
  • Drive letters: a Windows-style path can begin with a letter and colon, as in file:c:/path/to/file. Drive letter comparison is case insensitive.
  • Vertical line: some old URIs use | instead of :, as in file:///c|/path/to/file. To update such a URI, replace the vertical line with a colon.
  • UNC strings: a Windows UNC name can be mapped to the authority and path, so that \\host.example.com\Share\path\to\file.txt becomes file://host.example.com/Share/path/to/file.txt. Some software instead puts the whole UNC string in the path, as in file:////host.example.com/path/to/file.
  • Backslashes: pasted Windows paths may contain backslashes, which RFC 1738 and RFC 3986 forbid. They may be replaced by slashes if they were clearly meant as separators.
sections.plainLanguage: Over the years people wrote file addresses in some odd ways, especially on Windows. This part lists those habits and how to read or fix them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
File access and privileges are complex, and file URIs can complicate the security model. Historically, user agents have given content from the file scheme a tremendous amount of privilege, which can lead to privilege escalation attacks. Some user agents have granted directory-based privileges, with limited adoption. Others use a globally unique identifier as the origin for each file URI, which the RFC calls the most secure option.

Treating a non-local file URI as local, or attempting local operations on one, can cause security problems. File systems also give special meaning to characters such as /, \, :, [ and ], and to device names such as ., .., aux and lpt. Merely testing for such a name can make the operating system pause or make unrelated system calls, leading to denial of service or unintended data transfer. Implementers should research the reserved names for the storage they support.

Differences in case handling and Unicode equivalence can cause unexpected aliasing between paths or URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting a web page open any file on your computer is risky. Programs should be careful about files that are on other computers and about odd file names that make the computer do strange things.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers file as a permanent URI scheme, and the URI Schemes registry has been updated. The registration says the scheme is commonly used in hypertext documents to refer to files without depending on network access, and that major browsers support it. The change controller is the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: The name "file" was officially written into the list of address types, so everyone agrees it exists.

data.title: File URI grammar
data.code:
file-URI       = file-scheme ":" file-hier-part
file-scheme    = "file"
file-hier-part = ( "//" auth-path )
               / local-path
auth-path      = [ file-auth ] path-absolute
local-path     = path-absolute
file-auth      = "localhost"
               / host
